title: Deadly cop shooting puzzles kin ; Can't understand how charitable man ended up in ditch along Hwy. 417
article: The 43-year-old man shot to death by Ottawa police last week was the baby of a Sudbury family of 11 kids.
Richard Bastien's siblings want to know why their "baby brother" ended up lying in a ditch with a police bullet in his chest.

Bastien, a dental lab technician, allegedly shot his employer, 65-year-old Carp denturist Rainer Elsner, in the head, back and arm at Elsner's home on Bear Hill Rd. on April 22. It is alleged Bastien then led police on a high-speed chase along Hwy. 417 before ditching his car near Walkley Rd.
A standoff ensued, the province's Special Investigations Unit says, and Bastien was shot. He died at the Ottawa Hospital's Civic campus two days later. The SIU recovered a handgun from the scene.
Bastien's siblings can't understand how the life of a man who organized an annual charity golf tournament to provide underprivileged kids with school supplies could have ended this way.
"We'll never understand what happened because he's the only one who can tell us," said Jacky Armstrong, Bastien's eldest sister.
Bastien's "moods" changed when his 79-year-old mother died in 2005, she said.
"He was really close to my mom," Armstrong remembered.
Bastien's niece, Laura Armstrong, who sat sharing smokes and a ham sandwich in the kitchenette of her mother's Gatineau apartment yesterday, said she suspects police did "what they had to do."
"Obviously, he had made some bad choices. That poor officer who had to do that, imagine what he's going through?" she said.
But Bastien's first cousin, who didn't want to be named, thinks there had to be a better way for police to stop a desperate man.
"Did they really have to put a bullet in his head?" he asked. "I can understand if he shot somebody, he has to be stopped, but that doesn't mean you have to kill him."
Bastien had been living with his fiancee Roxanne, a massage therapist. They had recently moved from their Gatineau house to Laval.
Jacky Armstrong remembered Bastien showing off the landscaping he'd done when she went to their Gatineau home for a spaghetti dinner.
Relatives fondly remembered the "cow song" he liked to perform around the campfire.
Elsner told neighbours and friends Bastien had forged company cheques and stolen $20,000 while he was vacationing in Germany.
Bastien had come to Elsner's lab that day to talk about "the money." When Elsner told him the issue was in the hands of police, shots rang out.
Elsner, who is still in hospital, refused repeated requests for an interview. An employee answered the phone at his lab this week, but refused to talk.
"That's Rainer's story to tell, not mine," she said.
Bastien's funeral service will be held Saturday at 2 p.m. at Cooperative Funeraire in Gatineau.
